title: Range-Based for Loops
learningObjectives: Explain range-based for loops and their execution flow.
Trace condition checks and state changes across iterations.
Select a suitable loop structure for a given problem.
Identify common termination and boundary mistakes.
Apply the loop pattern in an original small program.

understand.concept: Range-based for visits each element in a range without requiring a manual index. Use const auto& for read-only access and auto& for in-place changes.
understand.whyItMatters: It reduces index mistakes and makes element-oriented intent clear.
understand.explain: Choose value, const reference, or mutable reference depending on whether copying or modification is needed.

examples.title: Read array
examples.explanation: Visits each element; scalar copies are inexpensive.

examples.title: Sum vector
examples.code: std::vector<int> v{5,10,15}; int sum=0;\nfor(int item:v) sum+=item;
examples.explanation: A direct element loop is sufficient when index is not needed.

examples.title: Transform array
examples.explanation: Mutable references let each element change.

practise.guidedTask: Trace and annotate each of the five Range-Based for Loops examples. For every iteration, record the relevant variable values, condition result and action. Change one input or bound and predict the new behavior.
practise.independentTask: Write a small C++ program demonstrating range-based for loops in a practical scenario. Include at least three typical tests, two boundary tests, and one invalid or termination test. Explain how the loop terminates.
hints: Use const auto& for read-only large elements.
Use auto& only when modifying elements.
Use plain auto for small inexpensive values.
No manual index is needed for element visits.

questions.explanation: const reference binds without copying and cannot mutate.
